summary: Maurice Lehot was an Indology scholar who studied at the University of Lyon under Félix Lacôte. He worked as a schoolteacher (Professor) at the Lycée d'Aix-en-Provence.

Maurice Leroy was a linguist who earned his doctorate at the Université libre de Bruxelles and studied under Theodor Bloch, Joseph Vendryes, and Émile Benveniste at the École Pratique des Hautes Études. He became ordinary professor at Bruxelles (1945).

Maurice O'Connell Walshe worked in Buddhist studies and linguistics, studying at UCL, Humboldt, Göttingen, Vienna, and under Walpola Rahula. He taught German at UCL, Leeds, Nottingham, and Bedford College, and served as Deputy Director at the University of London.

Maurice Phillips was an Indology and religious studies scholar educated at Bedford College and the University of Bern (Ph.D.). He served as a missionary with the London Missionary Society (1862–1908) and was a Fellow of the University of Madras.
Maurice Wiles was a religious studies scholar who studied at Tonbridge School and Christ's College, Cambridge. He later taught Michael Pye.
Maurice Wilmotte was a linguistics scholar who studied at the University of Liège from 1879 to 1883 and later held a post there from around 1895 to 1931.

Maurine Stuart was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at the University of Manitoba and under Nadia Boulanger, Eido Shimano, Hakuun Ryoko Yasutani, and Soen Nakagawa. In 1979, she became president and spiritual director of the Cambridge Buddhist Association.

Maurizio Taddei worked in history, archaeology, Indology, and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied under Mario Bussagli at Sapienza University, worked at the Museo Nazionale d'Arte Orientale, and taught Indian art and archaeology at the University of Naples "L'Orientale."

Mauro Maggi is a scholar of Iranian, Central Asian, Buddhist, and linguistic studies. He studied at the University of Naples "L'Orientale" and under Ronald Eric Emmerick, later holding posts at Sapienza University and the Italian Institute for Africa and the East.

Mavis L. Fenn specializes in Buddhist and religious studies. She studied at the Universities of Winnipeg, Calgary, and McMaster under Graeme MacQueen, later holding posts at St. Paul's University College and the University of Waterloo.
Max Arthur Macauliffe was an Indology and religious studies scholar who was educated at Springfield College and the University of Galway.

Max Deeg is an Indologist, Sinologist, and Buddhist studies scholar who completed his Habilitation at the University of Würzburg. He has held academic posts at Nagoya University, the University of Vienna, and Cardiff University.

Max Hunter Harrison was a religious studies and Indology scholar who studied at Knox College, Andover Newton, Harvard, and Columbia. He taught at Jaffna College and served as Principal of the United Theological College, Bangalore.

Max Jakob Niedermann was a linguist who studied at Zurich, Basel, and under Jacob Wackernagel, Antoine Meillet, Louis Havet, and Rudolf Thurneysen. He served as professor at the University of Basel and the University of Neuchâtel.

Max Kaltenmark was a scholar of Sinology and religious studies who held posts at the Centre Franco-Chinois d'Études Sinologiques, the University of Paris, the École française d'Extrême-Orient, and the École Pratique des Hautes Études.

Max Leopold Margolis was a scholar of linguistics and religious studies who earned his Ph.D. at Columbia. He held posts at Columbia, Hebrew Union College, the University of California, Berkeley, and Dropsie College.
Max Lindenau was an Indologist who studied at Munich, Greifswald, and Leipzig under Ernst Windisch. He later served as Privatdozent at the University of Marburg from 1919 to 1927.

Max Oidtmann is a historian, Sinologist, and Tibetologist who studied at Carleton College, Indiana University, and Harvard under Mark Elliott. He held faculty posts at Georgetown University in Qatar and the University of Munich.

Max Scheler was a philosopher who studied at the universities of Munich, Berlin, and Jena. He held academic posts at the University of Jena, the University of Munich, the University of Göttingen, and the University of Cologne.

Max Walleser, a scholar of Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy, studied at Heidelberg, Freiburg, Geneva, and Erlangen-Nuremberg. He founded the Walleser-Institut and served as extraordinary professor of Indian philology at Heidelberg University.
